title: Write test cases for a login page BEYOND the happy path: valid/invalid username, invalid password, both invalid, empty fields, password masking, account lockout after N failed attempts, remember-me, session timeout, logout, SQL-injection and XSS inputs, password reset, browser compatibility, accessibility, and precise error messages: and what is the interviewer actually evaluating (that you think past "login works")?
shortTitle: Writing login page test cases beyond the happy path
keyPoints: The happy path is one case; everything valuable lies in the negative, security, session, recovery, and non-functional cases around it
Negative credential matrix: valid user with wrong password, unknown user, both invalid, empty fields, all returning the same generic message
Security: account lockout after N attempts, SQL-injection and XSS inputs rejected, password masking, no enumeration leaks
Session: remember-me with secure cookies, session timeout after idle, logout invalidates server session so back button is safe
Recovery: password-reset link is single-use and time-limited, does not reveal whether the email exists
The interviewer evaluates breadth of thinking and risk awareness, not just whether login works

s1_definition.oneliner: Login testing beyond the happy path covers negatives, empty fields, masking, lockout, remember-me, session timeout, logout, injection and scripting attacks, password reset, browser and accessibility checks, and precise non-leaky error messages, because the interviewer is checking that you anticipate failure and abuse, not just success.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Happy path** – Valid credentials lead to the dashboard. This is one single case out of dozens.
- **Negative credential matrix** – Invalid username, invalid password, both invalid, empty fields, whitespace-only input, each returning the same generic error message to prevent account enumeration.
- **Security** – Account lockout after N failed attempts, SQL-injection and XSS inputs safely rejected, password masking, no information leaks.
- **Session** – Remember-me with secure cookies, session timeout after idle, logout that invalidates the server session.
- **Recovery** – Password-reset link that is single-use, time-limited, and does not reveal whether the email exists.
- **Non-functional** – Browser compatibility across the supported matrix, accessibility with keyboard navigation, ARIA roles, and screen-reader announcements.
s1_definition.analogy: For the National Bank of India login screen, the happy path is Rajesh typing his correct username and password and getting in. But a real tester asks all the uncomfortable questions: what if the password is wrong, what if both fields are empty, what if someone tries the wrong password ten times to break in, does the password show as dots so a shoulder-surfer cannot read it, does "remember me" actually keep him logged in, does the session expire after inactivity so an unattended machine is safe, can an attacker type a database trick or a script into the username box, and does the error message say just "invalid credentials" rather than revealing whether the username exists. Covering all of these is what separates a real tester from someone who only checks that the front door opens for the right key.

sections.s6_takeaway:
When I write login test cases I start from the position that the happy path, valid username and valid password leading to the dashboard, is a single case, and that everything valuable lies around it. I group the rest into families: negative credentials covering wrong password, unknown user, both invalid, and empty fields, all returning the same generic message so attackers cannot enumerate accounts; security covering account lockout at the boundary, SQL-injection and XSS inputs safely rejected, and password masking; session covering remember-me, timeout, and logout that fully invalidates the server session; recovery covering single-use, time-limited password-reset links; and non-functional covering browser compatibility and accessibility.

What the interviewer is really evaluating is whether I think past "login works." Anyone can confirm the front door opens for the right key; a strong tester enumerates how the feature fails and how it is abused, prioritizes by risk, and writes each case with precise preconditions, data, steps, and an exact expected result.

At the National Bank of India I owned the login test suite, and I caught two real issues: a response that revealed whether a username existed, which I flagged as an account-enumeration vulnerability, and a logout that did not invalidate the server session so the back button still showed account data. Both were missed by happy-path testing and both mattered because this was the front door to customers' money.

Being able to lay out these case families and explain the risk behind each, especially the security and session ones, is exactly how I show an interviewer I test like someone who protects a bank, not someone who checks a checkbox.

Remember one sentence: the happy path is one case, the other thirty cases covering negatives, security, sessions, and recovery are where the real testing lives.
